title: Memory Session — the bakery years
objective: Measure whether the memory-prompt-session craftbook banks a recorded session in the teller's own words, files it in the store, and produces real follow-up threads.
prompt: i recorded a long chat with mom about her bakery years — transcript is in recordings/session3.txt. can you file it as a sesion and tell me what to ask next time?

files.content:
Session 3 — recorded 2026-07-17, kitchen table. Teller: Mam (Els). Interviewer: Jip.

JIP: You always call them the bakery years. Start wherever you want.

ELS: We took over the bakery on the Vissersdijk in 1978. Your father signed the papers with flour already on his sleeves, that is how sure he was. I was twenty-six and I had never once seen four o'clock in the morning. By that first winter I could tell the time by the ovens without looking at a clock.

JIP: What did the mornings feel like?

ELS: Cold, then warm. That was the whole day, cold then warm. The front of the shop was ice until the ovens caught up. I kneaded with my coat on until six. The smell of the first proof — that is the smell I will want on my last day, I think. Yeast and warm linen.

JIP: Who came in?

ELS: Everyone came in. The harbor men at five thirty, before anyone else was awake. They never spoke before the first roll, not one word, and I learned not to speak either. Mrs. Terpstra every Thursday for the raisin loaf, and she paid in coins she counted twice. Children after school with their cents pressed flat and sweaty in their hands.

JIP: Was it ever bad?

ELS: The strike year was bad. I will not dress it up. Nineteen eighty-four, the flour price doubled in one season and we did not sleep for the mathematics of it. Your father wanted to sell. I said the ovens stay lit, and I took in mending in the afternoons so they could. Nobody in the town knew that. I did the mending in the back room with the curtain closed.

JIP: I never knew that either.

ELS: You were four. You knew the mixing bowl and the licking spoon, that was your whole world. You used to sleep in the flour sacks like a cat. The customers asked after you like you were part of the inventory.

JIP: Why did it end?

ELS: My hands, mostly. And the supermarket on the ring road, a little. We sold in 1990 to the Boonstra boy, who let it become a phone shop, which I have decided not to be bitter about. I kept the shop bell. It is in the box under the stairs with the wedding things. When I shake it I am twenty-six again, cold then warm.

JIP: We should stop, your tea is cold.

ELS: The tea is always cold when the talking is good. Next time I will tell you about the wedding cakes. The ones I made and the one I never got to make. Ask me about that one, will you? Do not let me wriggle out of it.

[recording ends 58:14]

# Els — timeline coverage

- 1950s — childhood on the dike: covered (session 1)
- 1960s — school years, first job: thin, one anecdote only
- 1971-1977 — meeting Pa, early marriage: covered (session 2)
- 1978-1990 — the bakery years: BIGGEST GAP, nothing banked yet
- 1990s — after the bakery: nothing
